notes.front: What is a sectional chart, in one sentence?
notes.back: The FAA’s main chart for visual flying: a 1:500,000 map of airports, airspace, obstructions and terrain.
notes.explanation: It is how you find out what airspace and hazards lie over a flying site before you decide whether, and how, you may fly there.
notes.example: Like a road atlas for the air: around Norfolk, Virginia, it shows the magenta rings of the Class C around the airport.
notes.source: FAA, Sectional Aeronautical Chart product page (Aeronautical Information Services)

notes.front: What is the FAA’s Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide, in one sentence?
notes.back: The FAA publication that explains the symbols on its aeronautical charts: a learning aid for new pilots and a quick reference.
notes.explanation: Chart symbols are occasionally added or changed (weather-camera symbols came to US sectionals in March 2026), so the current guide settles what any symbol means.
notes.example: Meet an unfamiliar magenta diamond marked ‘UA’ on a sectional? The guide’s ‘Miscellaneous Activity Areas’ explains it.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Introduction”, p. 6

notes.front: What is an airport data block on a sectional chart?
notes.back: The text printed beside an airport symbol: its name and identifier, frequencies, elevation, lighting and longest runway.
notes.explanation: Everything you need to know about an airport at a glance is coded here, so decoding it is a core chart skill.
notes.example: Garrison, North Dakota, reads ‘GARRISON (D05) 1937 *L 37 122.9 ©’: name, identifier, elevation, lighting, runway length, frequency.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: What is a CTAF, in one sentence?
notes.back: The Common Traffic Advisory Frequency: the frequency for airport advisory practices at an airport without an operating control tower.
notes.explanation: Manned pilots announce their positions on it, so it is how traffic near a non-towered airport is known; sectionals flag it with a circled C.
notes.example: Garrison’s data block shows ‘122.9 ©’, so 122.9 is its CTAF.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Non-towered Airport”, p. 65

notes.front: What is the Chart Supplement U.S., in one sentence?
notes.back: The FAA directory with the most comprehensive information on airports, heliports and seaplane bases open to the public.
notes.explanation: When a sectional says ‘see Chart Supplement’, for example about lighting limits or traffic patterns, the detail is in this directory.
notes.example: A ‘*L’ in a data block says lighting limitations exist; the airport’s Chart Supplement entry says what they are.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Chart Supplement U.S.”, p. 66

notes.front: On a sectional chart, what is a Class E vignette?
notes.back: A narrow shaded band marking where Class E airspace begins above the ground, either 700 ft or 1,200 ft AGL.
notes.explanation: Class E that starts above the ground is usually shown by a shaded band rather than a solid line; the colour of the fuzzy band tells you its floor, and so what lies beneath.
notes.example: The fuzzy magenta ring around Garrison, North Dakota, marks Class E beginning at 700 ft AGL.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 17

notes.front: What is a maximum elevation figure (MEF) on a sectional chart?
notes.back: The large figure in each quadrant giving the highest terrain or obstacle there, rounded up, in thousands and hundreds of feet MSL.
notes.explanation: It gives a quick sense of how high the ground and obstacles reach in an area. A quadrant is bounded by lines every 30 minutes of latitude and longitude.
notes.example: A large ‘13’ with a small ‘5’ means 13,500 ft MSL.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 12

notes.front: On a chart, what do latitude and longitude measure?
notes.back: Latitude: degrees north or south of the equator (parallels). Longitude: degrees east or west of the Prime Meridian (meridians).
notes.explanation: Any point can be located by its latitude and longitude, and sectionals are ruled with both.
notes.example: Washington, D.C. is about 39° N latitude, 77° W longitude; Chicago about 42° N, 88° W.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Latitude and Longitude (Meridians and Parallels)”, p. 68

notes.front: What is an isogonic line on a sectional chart?
notes.back: A broken magenta line joining places with equal magnetic variation, the angle between true north and magnetic north.
notes.explanation: Variation is labelled east or west, depending on whether magnetic north lies east or west of true north at that place.
notes.example: The agonic line is the one isogonic line along which variation is zero.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Variation”, p. 69

notes.front: What are chart abbreviations such as CT, RP, SFC and UC?
notes.back: CT = control tower, RP = right (traffic) pattern, SFC = surface, UC = under construction; the Chart Users’ Guide lists all abbreviations.
notes.explanation: These short forms are printed on aeronautical charts; later cards show where each appears.
notes.example: The guide’s legend names Class E airspace that starts at the surface “Class E (SFC)”, drawn as a magenta dashed line.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide, “Abbreviations and Acronyms”

notes.front: A sectional chart’s scale is {{c1::1:500,000}}: about 6.86 nautical miles, or roughly 8 statute miles, to the inch.
notes.explanation: The scale is large enough to show airports, airspace and obstacles in detail while still covering a wide area.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Sectional Charts”, p. 67

notes.front: How often are sectional charts updated?
notes.back: Every 56 days.
notes.explanation: The FAA’s chart page and the Chart Users’ Guide both say 56 days; the older Study Guide says ‘semiannually’, which is out of date.
notes.source: FAA, Sectional Aeronautical Chart product page (Aeronautical Information Services)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Sectional Aeronautical Chart page and Chart Users’ Guide (9 July 2026)

notes.front: What does the FAA say to do with obsolete charts?
notes.back: Always use current editions and discard obsolete charts; check NOTAMs for changes between chart editions.
notes.explanation: Aeronautical information changes quickly, so the chart’s next edition date on the cover tells you when it expires.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Keep Your Charts Current”, p. 6
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Sectional Aeronautical Chart page and Chart Users’ Guide (9 July 2026)

notes.front: Can you rely on a current sectional to show every new tower?
notes.back: No. A new tower may be missing because the information arrived after the chart was printed.
notes.explanation: Skeletal towers can exceed 1,000 ft AGL and their guy wires are hard to see, so look for them on site too.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Antenna Towers”, p. 69

notes.front: How is the Chart Supplement U.S. published, and how often is it revised?
notes.back: In seven regional books, revised every 56 days; it is also available online.
notes.explanation: It covers public-use airports, heliports and seaplane bases; a ‘Legend Sample’ at the front of each book explains how to decode entries.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Chart Supplement U.S.”, p. 14-3

notes.front: On a sectional chart, what colour are airports with a control tower, and what colour are all others?
notes.back: Towered airports and their data are blue; all other airports and their data are magenta.
notes.explanation: Colour is the quickest clue to whether an airport has an operating tower, which matters for the airspace around it.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

image.alt: Two airport symbols with data blocks from the Chart Users’ Guide. Left, in magenta: a runway symbol with a star labelled ‘Rotating Beacon in operation Sunset to Sunrise’, and below it ‘NAME (NAM) (PNAM)’, ‘ATIS 123.8’, ‘285 L 72 122.95’, ‘RP 23, 34’, with 122.95 marked UNICOM. Right, the same in blue for a towered airport, adding ‘FSS’, ‘NO SVFR’, ‘CT - 118.3 ★ © ATIS 123.8’, ‘VFR Advsy 125.0’ and ‘AOE’.
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 24

notes.front: In an airport data block, what does ‘CT - 118.3’ give?
notes.back: The control tower’s primary frequency, 118.3.
notes.explanation: ‘CT’ always means control tower, which is why these entries appear only in blue, towered-airport data blocks.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: In an airport data block, what does a star after the tower frequency mean?
notes.back: The tower operates part-time; the chart’s tower-frequency table gives its hours.
notes.explanation: Check the tabulated hours before assuming the tower is working.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: In an airport data block, what does a circled C after a frequency mean?
notes.back: That frequency is the airport’s CTAF.
notes.explanation: The Chart Users’ Guide shows the symbol as ‘Follows the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF)’.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: In the data block line ‘285 L 72 122.95’, what does 285 mean?
notes.back: The airport’s elevation: 285 ft MSL, the highest point of its usable landing area.
notes.explanation: Chart altitudes are in feet above mean sea level unless marked otherwise.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: In an airport data block, what is the difference between ‘L’ and ‘*L’?
notes.back: L: runway lights on from sunset to sunrise. *L: lighting limitations exist; see the Chart Supplement. A dash means no runway edge lights.
notes.explanation: Lighting codes refer to runway edge lights, which may not cover the longest runway or its full length.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: In the data block line ‘285 L 72 122.95’, what does 72 mean?
notes.back: The longest runway is about 7,200 ft: runway length is given in hundreds of feet.
notes.explanation: The usable length may be less than the charted length.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: What does ‘RP 23, 34’ in an airport data block mean?
notes.back: Runways 23 and 34 use right-hand traffic patterns. ‘*RP’ means see the Chart Supplement for special conditions.
notes.explanation: The pattern side tells you on which side of the runway manned traffic will be turning.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 16

notes.front: How is Class B airspace drawn on a sectional, and how are its altitudes shown?
notes.back: Solid blue lines; each sector shows its ceiling over its floor in hundreds of feet MSL, e.g. 100 over 40.
notes.explanation: Floors “upward from above” an altitude are preceded by a (+); operations at and below these altitudes are outside Class B.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

notes.front: How is Class C airspace drawn on a sectional, and how are its altitudes shown?
notes.back: Solid magenta lines; each sector shows its ceiling over its floor in hundreds of feet MSL, e.g. 48 over 30.
notes.explanation: The top number is the ceiling and the bottom the floor, so 48 over 30 means from 3,000 to 4,800 ft MSL.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

image.alt: Chart Users’ Guide legend for Class C: a magenta arc labelled ‘BURBANK CLASS C’ with the note ‘See NOTAMs/Directory for Class C eff hrs’; the figures 48 over 30 explained as ‘Ceiling of Class C in hundreds of feet MSL’ and ‘Floor of Class C in hundreds of feet MSL’; and a magenta box ‘CTC BURBANK APP WITHIN 20 NM ON 124.6 395.9’.
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 27

notes.front: In Class C altitude figures, what do ‘SFC’ and ‘T’ mean?
notes.back: SFC: the sector starts at the surface. T (as a ceiling): up to, but not including, the floor of the Class B above.
notes.explanation: So the Class C stops where the Class B begins.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

notes.front: How is Class D airspace drawn on a sectional, and how is its ceiling shown?
notes.back: A dashed blue line, with the ceiling in a dashed box in hundreds of feet MSL: [27] means 2,700 ft MSL.
notes.explanation: Class D surrounds towered airports, so its colour matches their blue data blocks.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

image.alt: Chart Users’ Guide legend for Class D: a dashed blue circle and extension with a dashed box ‘27’, notes ‘See NOTAMs/Supplement for Class D eff hrs’ and ‘Class D excluded below 1500’ MSL’; below, a dashed blue circle with the box ‘-27’ beside a dashed magenta extension, with the text ‘A minus in front of the figure is used to indicate “from surface to but not including...”’.
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 27

notes.front: What does a minus sign in a Class D ceiling box mean, e.g. [-27]?
notes.back: Class D from the surface up to, but not including, 2,700 ft MSL.
notes.explanation: The minus flags that the Class D stops just below the stated altitude rather than at it.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

notes.front: What does the note ‘See NOTAMs/Supplement for Class D eff hrs’ tell you?
notes.back: That Class D is not continuous: check NOTAMs or the Chart Supplement for the hours it is in effect.
notes.explanation: Class C and Class E surface areas that operate part-time carry the same kind of note.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

notes.front: How is Class E airspace that begins at the surface drawn on a sectional?
notes.back: A dashed magenta line.
notes.explanation: A Class E surface area designated for an airport is controlled airspace from the ground up.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 17

notes.front: What does a magenta Class E vignette mean?
notes.back: Class E airspace with a floor of 700 ft AGL.
notes.explanation: The magenta band marks the edge of the area where controlled airspace comes down to 700 ft above the ground.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 17

image.alt: Chart Users’ Guide legend of three shaded bands: a magenta band labelled ‘700’ Class E eff 0600-2300’ for ‘Airspace beginning at 700 feet AGL that laterally abuts 1200 feet or higher Class E Airspace’; a magenta band beside ‘CLASS G’ for ‘Airspace beginning at 700 feet AGL that laterally abuts uncontrolled (Class G) airspace’; and a blue band for ‘Airspace beginning at 1200 feet AGL that laterally abuts uncontrolled (Class G) airspace’.
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 27

notes.front: What does a blue Class E vignette mean?
notes.back: Class E airspace with a floor of 1,200 ft AGL, where it borders uncontrolled Class G.
notes.explanation: Blue vignettes typically mark the edge of wide uncontrolled areas.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 17

notes.front: Unless the chart shows otherwise, Class E airspace begins at {{c1::1,200 ft AGL}}.
notes.explanation: Where no vignette, dashed line or other floor is charted, this default applies; 700 ft floors are shown by a magenta vignette, and other floors by a blue vignette or a symbol and number.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 17

notes.front: On a sectional, how are prohibited, restricted and warning areas drawn?
notes.back: With blue hatched borders, labelled P-, R- or W- and a number.
notes.explanation: Blue marks the areas where flight is prohibited, or needs permission, or may be hazardous.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Chart Tabulations”, p. 20; legend, p. 30

image.alt: Chart Users’ Guide legend of three hatched boxes: a blue box reading ‘P-56 or R-6401 or W-518’ captioned ‘PROHIBITED, RESTRICTED or WARNING AREA’; a magenta box reading ‘ALERT AREA A-631 CONCENTRATED STUDENT HELICOPTER TRAINING’ captioned ‘ALERT AREA’; and a magenta box reading ‘VANCE 2 MOA’ with a note ‘VANCE 2 MOA EXCLUDES AIRSPACE 1500’ AGL AND BELOW’ captioned ‘MILITARY OPERATIONS AREA (MOA)’.
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 30

notes.front: On a sectional, how are alert areas and MOAs drawn?
notes.back: With magenta hatched borders: alert areas labelled A- and a number, MOAs by name (e.g. Vance 2 MOA).
notes.explanation: MOAs are named, not numbered; alert areas warn of heavy pilot training or unusual aerial activity.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Chart Tabulations”, p. 20; legend, p. 30

notes.front: Where on a sectional do you find a special use airspace’s altitudes, times of use and controlling agency?
notes.back: In the special use airspace tabulation printed on the chart.
notes.explanation: The table lists the controlling agency or contact facility and its frequency, which you need to seek permission to fly in a restricted area.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Chart Tabulations”, p. 20

notes.front: Is a NOTAM issued to announce a special use airspace’s permanently listed times of use?
notes.back: No. A NOTAM is not issued for times of use already listed on the chart.
notes.explanation: So read the chart’s tabulation as well as the NOTAMs.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Chart Tabulations”, p. 20

notes.front: How is a national security area shown on a sectional chart?
notes.back: With a broken magenta line, often with a notice asking pilots to avoid flight below a stated altitude.
notes.explanation: Pilots are asked to avoid flying through these areas, and flight in them may be temporarily prohibited.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Other Airspace Areas”, p. 18

image.alt: Chart Users’ Guide legend for a National Security Area: an arc of broken magenta dashes, a small magenta shape labelled ‘Small Area’, and a magenta notice box: ‘NOTICE FOR REASONS OF NATIONAL SECURITY PILOTS ARE REQUESTED TO AVOID FLIGHT BELOW 1200’ MSL IN THIS AREA’.
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 30

notes.front: Which temporary flight restrictions are drawn on a sectional chart?
notes.back: Only those relating to national security, shown with a broken blue line. All others you must find in NOTAMs.
notes.explanation: A TFR is a type of NOTAM, and the text of the actual TFR holds the details. (The legend also marks sporting-event TFR sites and long-running national-defense TFR areas; details are always in NOTAMs.)
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Other Airspace Areas”, p. 18; legend, pp. 30–31

notes.front: What should you do when a sectional shows a miscellaneous activity symbol, such as glider or parachute operations?
notes.back: Check NOTAMs before flight: the hazards vary widely, and the activity may share the area with regular flying.
notes.explanation: The symbols only mark where such activity happens; NOTAMs carry the details.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Other Airspace Areas”, p. 17

image.alt: Chart Users’ Guide list of Miscellaneous Activity Area symbols in magenta: Aerobatic Practice Area (diamond with A over a swoosh), Glider Operations (diamond with G), Hang Glider Activity (diamond with H), Ultralight Activity (diamond with U), Unmanned Aircraft Activity (diamond with UA), Parachute Jumping Area with Frequency (parachute and 122.9) and Space Launch Activity Area (rocket).
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 31

notes.front: On a sectional, a magenta diamond with the letter A over a swoosh marks {{c1::an aerobatic practice area}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Chart Users’ Guide’s miscellaneous activity area symbols; check NOTAMs for details.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Miscellaneous Activity Areas”, p. 31

notes.front: On a sectional, a magenta diamond with the letter G over a swoosh marks {{c1::glider operations}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Chart Users’ Guide’s miscellaneous activity area symbols; check NOTAMs for details.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Miscellaneous Activity Areas”, p. 31

notes.front: On a sectional, a magenta diamond with the letter H over a swoosh marks {{c1::hang glider activity}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Chart Users’ Guide’s miscellaneous activity area symbols; check NOTAMs for details.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Miscellaneous Activity Areas”, p. 31

notes.front: On a sectional, a magenta diamond with the letter U over a swoosh marks {{c1::ultralight activity}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Chart Users’ Guide’s miscellaneous activity area symbols; check NOTAMs for details.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Miscellaneous Activity Areas”, p. 31

notes.front: On a sectional, what does a magenta rocket symbol mark?
notes.back: A space launch activity area.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Chart Users’ Guide’s miscellaneous activity area symbols.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Miscellaneous Activity Areas”, p. 31

notes.front: How does a sectional show an obstacle’s height?
notes.back: The elevation of its top in feet MSL, with its height above the ground (AGL) in parentheses below.
notes.explanation: The AGL figure tells you how tall it is where you stand; in very congested areas the AGL value may be left off.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 11

image.alt: Chart Users’ Guide obstruction legend in blue: ‘Above 200’ & below 1000’ AGL (above 299’ AGL in urban area)’ shown as a small tower symbol with 1473 over (394) bldg; ‘Under Construction (UC) or reported and position/elevation unverified’ as 628 UC; ‘1000’ and higher (AGL)’ as a taller symbol with 3368 over (1529); ‘Wind Turbine’ as 2179 over (315); then High-Intensity Obstruction Lights symbols with rays for less than 1000’ AGL, 1000’ and higher, wind turbine, group obstruction and wind turbines, noting they may operate part-time or by proximity activation.
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 33

notes.front: What does ‘UC’ next to an obstacle on a sectional mean?
notes.back: Under construction, or reported but its position or elevation not yet verified.
notes.explanation: Treat the figures as uncertain and look for the obstacle on site.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 11

notes.front: Which man-made obstacles does a sectional normally show?
notes.back: Those more than 200 ft AGL, or more than 299 ft AGL within yellow city tint.
notes.explanation: Shorter obstacles, which a drone at up to 400 ft AGL could still hit, are generally not charted.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 11

notes.front: Does a sectional use the same symbol for obstacles 1,000 ft AGL or higher as for shorter ones?
notes.back: No. Obstacles 1,000 ft AGL and higher have their own, taller symbol.
notes.explanation: Separate symbols let you spot the tallest structures at a glance.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Obstruction”, p. 33

notes.front: In a high-density area such as a city, what does a group obstruction symbol show?
notes.back: Several obstacles close together; only the highest is charted, with its elevation.
notes.explanation: Grouping keeps the chart legible, so expect more obstacles than the symbol suggests.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 11

notes.front: Why can a lit wind turbine still surprise a low-flying aircraft?
notes.back: Its obstruction lights sit on the nacelle at the hub, which can be 200–300 ft below the blade tips, and the blades are unlit.
notes.explanation: Wind farms are charted as a hatched area with a boxed MSL elevation of the highest turbine.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 11

notes.front: What do ray-like lines drawn around an obstruction symbol mean?
notes.back: The obstruction has high-intensity lights, which may operate part-time or only when an aircraft is close.
notes.explanation: Proximity activation means the lights may be dark until something approaches.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “High-Intensity Obstruction Lights”, p. 33

notes.front: How do you read the maximum elevation figure shown as a large 13 and a small 5?
notes.back: 13,500 ft MSL.
notes.explanation: The large digits are thousands of feet and the small digit hundreds; the value is rounded up to the next 100 ft.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF)”, p. 33

image.alt: Chart Users’ Guide legend entry ‘Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF)’ showing a large blue ‘13’ followed by a smaller raised ‘5’.
image.credit: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), p. 33

notes.front: Is a maximum elevation figure verified by survey?
notes.back: No. It is based on the best information available, not on field surveys.
notes.explanation: For a natural high point the FAA adds 200 ft for uncharted obstacles before rounding up.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 13

notes.front: What is the agonic line on a chart?
notes.back: The line along which magnetic variation is zero: true north and magnetic north coincide.
notes.explanation: Isogonic lines join points of equal variation; the agonic line is the special case with none.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Variation”, p. 69

notes.front: Roughly between which latitudes do the 48 conterminous United States lie?
notes.back: Between 25° and 49° north.
notes.explanation: They lie between about 67° and 125° west longitude.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Latitude and Longitude (Meridians and Parallels)”, p. 68

notes.front: On a sectional chart, two points are 2 inches apart. About how far apart are they?
notes.back: About 13.7 nautical miles (roughly 16 statute miles).
notes.explanation: At 1:500,000 one inch is about 6.86 NM, or roughly 8 SM, so 2 inches is twice that.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Sectional Charts”, p. 67

notes.front: A remote PIC plans a job using a sectional printed four months ago. Is it still current?
notes.back: No. Sectionals are updated every 56 days, so at least one newer edition has been issued.
notes.explanation: Use the current edition and check NOTAMs for changes since it was published.
notes.source: FAA, Sectional Aeronautical Chart product page (Aeronautical Information Services)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Sectional Aeronautical Chart page and Chart Users’ Guide (9 July 2026)

notes.front: Figure: Norfolk. What airspace is inside the inner magenta circle marked 40 over SFC, and what must a remote pilot have to fly there?
notes.back: Class C from the surface to 4,000 ft MSL; prior authorization from ATC is required.
notes.explanation: Solid magenta lines mark Class C, and part 107 requires prior ATC authorization to operate in Class B, C or D airspace.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 20; 14 CFR § 107.41

notes.back: An alert area: it may contain a high volume of pilot training (here, student jet training). Exercise caution.
notes.explanation: Activity there follows the normal rules, and participating and transiting pilots are equally responsible for collision avoidance.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 2, “Alert Areas”, p. 9

notes.front: Figure: Maryland. What kind of special use airspace is the area labelled P-40?
notes.back: A prohibited area: flight of aircraft within it is prohibited.
notes.explanation: Prohibited areas are charted as ‘P’ plus a number; P-40 surrounds Camp David.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 2, “Prohibited Areas”, p. 7

notes.explanation: Only national-security TFRs are charted, as broken blue lines; the TFR’s NOTAM text holds its details.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) Relating to National Security”, p. 29

notes.front: On a sectional, what does this symbol mark?
notes.back: An area of unmanned aircraft activity.
notes.explanation: It is one of the miscellaneous activity area symbols; check NOTAMs for details before flying nearby.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Miscellaneous Activity Areas”, p. 31

notes.front: On a sectional, what does this symbol with a frequency mark?
notes.back: A parachute jumping area; the frequency is given with it.
notes.explanation: Frequently used jump sites are charted; others are published in the Chart Supplement.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Miscellaneous Activity Areas”, p. 31

notes.front: Your site lies inside a broken magenta line with a notice asking pilots to avoid flight below 1,200 ft MSL for national security. What is it and what should you do?
notes.back: A national security area: avoid flying there, and check NOTAMs, as flight may be temporarily prohibited.
notes.explanation: The request to avoid is advisory, but temporary prohibitions are issued by NOTAM.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 2, “National Security Areas (NSAs)”, p. 11

notes.front: A site lies inside a blue vignette, with no dashed lines nearby. You will fly at 350 ft AGL. Which airspace applies, and do you need ATC authorization?
notes.back: Class G (Class E starts at 1,200 ft AGL); no authorization is needed.
notes.choices:
A) Class E: authorization needed
B) Class G: no authorization needed
C) Class D: authorization needed
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class E starts only at 1,200 ft AGL here, above your flight. C: Class D is a dashed blue line, and none is charted.
notes.explanation: Below the 1,200 ft floor the airspace is uncontrolled.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 17

notes.front: A data block shows ‘*L’ and ‘*RP’. Where do you find what they mean for that airport?
notes.back: In the airport’s Chart Supplement entry.
notes.explanation: Both asterisks send you to the Chart Supplement, which describes lighting limitations and traffic-pattern restrictions.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Airports”, p. 15

notes.front: You need permission to fly in a restricted area. Where on the sectional do you find who controls it?
notes.back: In the chart’s special use airspace tabulation, which lists the controlling agency or contact facility.
notes.explanation: The tabulation also gives the area’s altitudes and times of use.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Chart Tabulations”, p. 20

notes.front: A 180 ft AGL tower stands next to your site in open country. Will the sectional show it?
notes.back: Probably not: sectionals normally chart man-made obstacles only above 200 ft AGL.
notes.explanation: Always survey the site; the chart is not a complete obstacle list.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 11

notes.front: Your site is next to a glider-operations symbol on the sectional. What should you do before flying?
notes.back: Check NOTAMs, and expect glider activity alongside regular flying.
notes.explanation: Miscellaneous activity symbols mark where such activity happens; NOTAMs give the details.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Other Airspace Areas”, p. 17

notes.front: A sectional shows no TFR over a stadium where a big event is planned. Can you assume there is none?
notes.back: No. Only national-security TFRs are charted; check NOTAMs for any other TFR.
notes.explanation: The chart may mark a stadium as a sporting-event TFR site, but whether a TFR is active, and its limits and times, is only in the NOTAM, so check NOTAMs.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Other Airspace Areas”, p. 18; legend, pp. 30–31

notes.front: You need an airport’s full details, such as lighting limits and services. Which publication do you use?
notes.back: The Chart Supplement U.S.
notes.explanation: The sectional gives a summary in the data block; the Chart Supplement is the most comprehensive source on an airport.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 11, “Chart Supplement U.S.”, p. 66

notes.front: The maximum elevation figure for your quadrant is a large 2 and a small 4. What does it tell you?
notes.back: The highest terrain or obstacle in that quadrant is expected to be at or below 2,400 ft MSL.
notes.explanation: The figure is rounded up to the next 100 ft and includes a margin for error.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 12

notes.front: On a sectional, what is the difference between a dashed blue line and a dashed magenta line?
notes.back: Dashed blue: Class D. Dashed magenta: Class E beginning at the surface.
notes.explanation: Both mark controlled airspace from the surface that needs ATC authorization under part 107.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

notes.front: On a sectional, what is the difference between solid blue and solid magenta airspace lines?
notes.back: Solid blue: Class B. Solid magenta: Class C.
notes.explanation: Both show sector altitudes as ceiling over floor in hundreds of feet MSL.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

notes.front: Magenta vignette versus blue vignette: what floor does each mark?
notes.back: Magenta: Class E from 700 ft AGL. Blue: Class E from 1,200 ft AGL next to Class G.
notes.explanation: Below either floor, outside any surface area, the airspace is Class G.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 17

notes.front: Special use airspace with blue hatching versus magenta hatching: which types does each colour show?
notes.back: Blue: prohibited, restricted and warning areas. Magenta: alert areas and MOAs.
notes.explanation: Part 107 requires the using or controlling agency’s permission to fly in prohibited or restricted areas.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Chart Tabulations”, p. 20; legend, p. 30

notes.front: A broken magenta line versus a broken blue line around an area: what does each mark?
notes.back: Broken magenta: a national security area. Broken blue: a temporary flight restriction relating to national security.
notes.explanation: Both relate to security; the TFR is a NOTAM restriction, the NSA a request to avoid. (The legend also marks sporting-event TFR sites and national-defense TFR areas; details are always in NOTAMs.)
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Other Airspace Areas”, p. 18

notes.front: Class D ceiling box [27] versus [-27]: what is the difference?
notes.back: [27]: Class D up to 2,700 ft MSL. [-27]: from the surface up to, but not including, 2,700 ft MSL.
notes.explanation: The minus means the stated altitude itself is not part of the Class D.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Controlled Airspace”, p. 16

notes.front: On an obstacle label such as 1473 (394), which number is MSL and which AGL?
notes.back: 1473 is the top’s elevation in feet MSL; (394) in parentheses is its height in feet AGL.
notes.explanation: For a drone limited by height above the ground, the AGL figure is the one to compare.
notes.source: FAA Aeronautical Information Services, Aeronautical Chart Users’ Guide (effective 9 July 2026), “Land Features (Terrain) and Obstructions”, p. 11
